knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: 5.1.1
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly states Bayes' theorem connecting prior, likelihood, and posterior?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Bayes updates by combining prior and likelihood into a normalised posterior.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Posterior proportional to prior times likelihood (normalised).
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Skipping the prior-likelihood product or equating inverse conditionals.

choices.label: Posterior is proportional to prior times likelihood (then normalised). Bayes updates beliefs about an event or parameter given the data.
Posterior equals the likelihood alone; the prior is discarded once data arrive.
Posterior equals the prior alone; likelihood is used only for frequentist tests.
Bayes equates P(A|B) with P(B|A) automatically, so prior and likelihood need not be combined.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: 5.1.1
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly refuses treating P(disease|positive) as equal to P(positive|disease) without calculation?
knowledge_checks.body: Refuse inverse confusion; state what Bayes requires.
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Inverse probability confusion ignores base rates; Bayes combines prior and likelihood.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Refuse equating the inverse conditionals; combine prior (base rate) with likelihood.

choices.label: Refuse inverse confusion. The two conditionals are not equal. Bayes combines a prior (base rate) with the likelihood of the data to obtain the posterior.
Accept the equality because positive tests and disease status are interchangeable labels.
Refuse only when base rates are unknown; if prevalence is known, P(disease|positive) equals P(positive|disease) automatically.
Bayes requires replacing the prior with the likelihood alone, which makes the two conditionals equal after any positive test.
